reason: The hypothesis relies on the formation of a uniform, ultrathin oxide layer that limits diffusion and prevents segregation in nanoparticles. The cited evidence (E1) describes oxidation of bulk alloys over long timescales, leading to layered, non-uniform oxides and subsurface elemental depletion due to outward cation diffusion—mechanisms that contradict the proposed uniform, diffusion-limiting passivation layer. No evidence is provided for controlled ultrathin oxide formation on nanoparticles or its effect on surface diffusion.
premises: An ultrathin, uniform oxide layer can form on near-equiatomic low noble-metal nanoparticles under controlled low-pO2 oxidation.
This oxide layer acts as a physical barrier that limits surface diffusion.
Limiting surface diffusion inhibits elemental segregation and particle coarsening at high temperatures.
The cited evidence (E1) on bulk alloy oxidation supports the formation of protective oxide layers that alter near-surface composition.
